section.title: Jerusalem's Refusal to Repent
section.sectionRationale: This unit presses the covenant lawsuit further by testing the city itself: can even one person of justice and truth be found, from the poor to the powerful. The universal failure justifies the coming disaster, while the closing scene exposes leaders and people alike as content with comfortable lies.
section.thesis: Not one person in Jerusalem, poor or powerful, can be found who acts justly and seeks truth, so the LORD brings a fearsome, ancient nation against a people who love false prophets and corrupt priests more than the truth.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the search for a single just person in Jerusalem's streets; the ancient, mighty nation summoned as instrument of judgment; the foolish, senseless people who neither see nor hear; and the wicked among the people who prosper by deceit while priests rule by their own authority.

units.label: Search for one just person
units.note: not one who seeks the truth

verses.text: “Go up and down the streets of Jerusalem. Look now and take note; search her squares. If you can find a single person, anyone who acts justly, anyone who seeks the {{emet|truth}}, then I will forgive the city.
Although they say, ‘As surely as the LORD lives,’ they are swearing falsely.”

O LORD, do not Your eyes look for truth? You struck them, but they felt no pain. You finished them off, but they refused to accept discipline. They have made their faces harder than stone and refused to repent.
Then I said, “They are only the poor; they have played the fool, for they do not know the way of the LORD, the justice of their God.

I will go to the powerful and speak to them. Surely they know the way of the LORD, the justice of their God.” 
But they too, with one accord, had broken the yoke and torn off the chains.

Therefore a lion from the forest will strike them down, a wolf from the desert will ravage them. A leopard will lie in wait near their cities, and everyone who ventures out will be torn to pieces. For their rebellious acts are many, and their unfaithful deeds are numerous.

“Why should I forgive you? Your children have forsaken Me 
and sworn by gods that are not gods. I satisfied their needs, yet they committed adultery and assembled at the houses of prostitutes.
They are well-fed, lusty stallions, each neighing after his neighbor's wife.
Should I not punish them for these things?” declares the LORD. “Should I not avenge Myself on such a nation as this?

units.label: An ancient nation summoned
units.note: an established nation whose language you do not know

verses.text: Go up through her vineyards and ravage them, but do not finish them off. Strip off her branches, for they do not belong to the LORD.
For the house of Israel and the house of Judah have been utterly unfaithful to Me,” declares the LORD.

They have lied about the LORD and said: 
“He will not do anything; harm will not come to us; we will not see sword or famine.

The prophets are but wind, for the word is not in them. 
So let their own predictions befall them.”

Therefore this is what the LORD God of Hosts says: 
“Because you have spoken this word, I will make My words a fire in your mouth 
and this people the wood it consumes.

Behold, I am bringing a distant nation against you, O house of Israel,” declares the LORD. “It is an established nation, an ancient nation, a nation whose language you do not know and whose speech you do not understand.
Their quivers are like open graves; they are all mighty men.

They will devour your harvest and food; they will consume your sons and daughters; they will eat up your flocks and herds; they will feed on your vines and fig trees. With the sword they will destroy the fortified cities in which you trust.”
“Yet even in those days,” declares the LORD, “I will not make a full end of you.

And when the people ask, ‘For what offense has the LORD our God done all these things to us?’ You are to tell them, ‘Just as you have forsaken Me and served foreign gods in your land, so will you serve foreigners in a land that is not your own.’”

units.label: Foolish and senseless
units.note: eyes that do not see, ears that do not hear

verses.text: Declare this in the house of Jacob and proclaim it in Judah:
“Hear this, O {{nabal|foolish}} and senseless people, who have eyes but do not see, who have ears but do not hear.

Do you not fear Me?” declares the LORD. “Do you not tremble before Me, the One who set the sand as the boundary for the sea, 
an enduring barrier it cannot cross? The waves surge, but they cannot prevail. They roar but cannot cross it.
But these people have stubborn and rebellious hearts. They have turned aside and gone away.
They have not said in their hearts, ‘Let us fear the LORD our God, who gives the rains, both autumn and spring, in season, who keeps for us the appointed weeks of harvest.’
Your iniquities have diverted these from you; your sins have deprived you of My bounty.

units.label: Wicked among my people
units.note: prophets prophesy falsely, priests rule by their own authority

verses.text:
For among My people are wicked men; they watch like fowlers lying in wait; 
they set a trap to catch men.

Like cages full of birds, so their houses are full of deceit. 
Therefore they have become powerful and rich.

They have grown fat and sleek, and have excelled in the deeds of the wicked. They have not taken up the cause of the fatherless, that they might prosper; nor have they defended the rights of the needy.
Should I not punish them for these things?” declares the LORD. “Should I not avenge Myself on such a nation as this?
A horrible and shocking thing has happened in the land.
The prophets prophesy falsely, and the priests rule by their own authority. My people love it so, but what will you do in the end?

emet.gloss: Truth, faithfulness, reliability. God's search of Jerusalem's streets is not for perfection but for even one person who genuinely seeks and lives by emet, showing how far a hollow, oath-swearing religiosity had drifted from real integrity before God.

nabal.gloss: Foolish, senseless, morally obtuse rather than merely intellectually slow. This is the same root used of the fool who says in his heart there is no God, Psalm 14:1, describing a willful blindness that has eyes and ears yet refuses to see or hear the obvious evidence of God.

basic.context: God sends Jeremiah on a search through Jerusalem's streets: can even one person be found who acts justly and seeks truth? From the poorest to the most powerful, the answer is no, and so an ancient, terrifying nation whose language no one understands is summoned as the LORD's chosen instrument of judgment. The chapter ends by exposing the whole religious system, prophets who lie and priests who rule by their own authority, propped up by a people who actually prefer it that way.
basic.hermeneutics: This is prophetic covenant lawsuit language building toward a specific historical judgment, the coming Babylonian invasion, framed as both deserved punishment and revelation of just how deep and universal Judah's corruption had become. The uncomfortable honesty here is verse 31, my people love it so, this is not a people deceived against their will but one that actively prefers comfortable lies to hard truth, and Scripture does not let that be softened.
basic.originalLanguages: God searches for anyone who seeks emet, truth or faithfulness, not abstract correctness but a reliable, trustworthy life lived before Him; none is found. By verse 21 the people are called nabal, foolish, the same word used of the fool who says in his heart there is no God, describing not low intelligence but willful spiritual blindness in those who have eyes and ears yet refuse to use them.
basic.typology: The vain search for a single righteous person in Jerusalem anticipates Paul's sweeping indictment that none is righteous, no, not one, Romans 3:10, a universal diagnosis this passage previews on a smaller, national scale. Only in Christ, the one truly righteous man, is the search this chapter fails to complete finally answered.
basic.christ: Where Jeremiah cannot find one just person in all of Jerusalem, the New Testament identifies the one man in whom perfect justice and truth are finally found, Christ, who alone fulfills what verse 1 searches for in vain and who alone can forgive not merely a spared city but a redeemed people. Paul's universal indictment in Romans 3:10-18 draws on exactly this kind of prophetic search coming up empty, resolved only in the righteousness given through faith in Jesus.
basic.god: God is patient and searching, willing to forgive the entire city for the sake of even one faithful person, yet unflinchingly honest about what that search reveals: total, willful unfaithfulness from the poorest to the most powerful. His judgment through a foreign, terrifying nation is severe, yet even here He limits it, I will not make a full end.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 18:22-33 has Abraham similarly plead for Sodom on the basis of finding even a few righteous people. Romans 3:10-18 gives Paul's universal verdict, none is righteous, echoing the failed search of this chapter on a global scale. Psalm 14:1-3 uses the same picture of fools who do not seek God. Habakkuk 1:5-11 similarly describes a fierce, foreign nation raised up as God's instrument of judgment.
basic.oneStory: This is the moment the covenant lawsuit becomes a citywide verdict: not one person can be found who lives by truth and justice, so judgment through a foreign power becomes necessary and just. That universal failure, previewed here in one city, is diagnosed for the whole human race in Romans, and answered only in Christ, the one righteous man whose life and death make forgiveness possible for all who trust Him.

context.literary:
Chapter 5 sits between two alarms. Chapter 4 sounded the trumpet and described the north wind of invasion; chapter 6 will show the siege ramps going up. In between, chapter 5 answers the question every hearer would ask: why? It is the book's courtroom chapter, and it is built like a trial with a search for evidence, a verdict, a sentence, and an exchange about the sentence.

The search of verses 1 to 9 is a descending scale. Jeremiah looks first among the poor, who might be excused as ignorant, verse 4, then among the powerful, who have no excuse, verse 5, and finds the same thing at both ends. The detail that matters is the last line of verse 5. The leaders had 'broken the yoke and torn off the chains,' which is covenant language. The yoke and bonds are the picture of Israel's obligation to God, and Leviticus 26:13 uses the same figure for what God broke when He freed them from Egypt. Judah has broken the one yoke that was never heavy.

Verses 9 and 29 are the same two questions word for word, 'Should I not punish them for these things? Should I not avenge Myself on such a nation as this?' That refrain frames the whole middle of the chapter and divides it into two indictments, one on the people's worship and speech, the other on the people's economics and their leaders. Inside the frame the pace changes from the short stabs of verses 1 to 9, to the long marching description of the invaders in 15 to 17, to the slow creation hymn of 22 to 24 about sea, sand and seasonal rain.

Voices keep switching. The LORD speaks, Jeremiah answers in verses 3 to 5, the LORD speaks again, and in verse 19 Jeremiah is handed a script for a future conversation: when the people ask why, tell them. The last line is a question that has no answer written under it, 'what will you do in the end?' The chapter ends with the hearer, not with God.
context.historical:
The chapter is undated. It belongs somewhere in the long middle of Jeremiah's ministry, which began in the thirteenth year of Josiah, Jeremiah 25:3, and ran through the fall of the city. Readers differ on whether these words were first spoken before or after Josiah's reform, which began when the Book of the Law was found in the temple, 2 Kings 22:8. The charges in verses 2 and 7, empty oath formulas and worship of 'gods that are not gods,' fit a people for whom reform had been mostly surface, and Jeremiah's own later comment is that Judah did not return 'with all her heart,' Jeremiah 3:10. Whatever the date, the political setting is Judah's confidence that Zion was safe. Within living memory Jerusalem had been spared from Sennacherib in 701, 2 Kings 19:35, and the verse 12 slogan, 'harm will not come to us,' grows out of that story and the songs about God dwelling in her, Psalm 46:5.

Verses 26 to 28 show the social order behind the religious one. The 'wicked men' are not bandits but the well fed. They build houses 'full of deceit' and grow fat on the fatherless and the needy, the very groups the law named for protection, Exodus 22:21-22. The trapping language of bird catchers pictures fraud and the courts used against people who cannot defend themselves.

The rain language in verse 24 is pointed. In the Canaanite religion Baal was the storm and rain god, and the early rains and late rains were his gift. Jeremiah's God claims them. It is He 'who gives the rains, both autumn and spring, in season, who keeps for us the appointed weeks of harvest,' as Deuteronomy 11:14 had promised. To worship Baal in a land watered by YHWH is to thank the wrong benefactor.

The invader of verse 15, 'a nation whose language you do not know,' echoes the curse of Deuteronomy 28:49. When Jeremiah speaks, the rising power is Babylon, a people whose Akkadian speech would have been unintelligible to ordinary Judeans. Even Aramaic, the language of diplomacy, was kept from the people on the wall, 2 Kings 18:26.
context.canonical:
The search in verse 1 stands in a line of divine searches. In Genesis 18:23-32 Abraham bargains down from fifty to ten righteous people to save Sodom. Jeremiah's version has no bargaining and a much lower number, a single person, and still the city is not spared, because none is found. Ezekiel, writing for the exiles, tells the same sad story from God's side: 'I searched for a man among them to repair the wall and stand in the gap before Me on behalf of the land, so that I should not destroy it. But I found no one,' Ezekiel 22:30. Isaiah goes further: 'The LORD looked and was displeased that there was no justice,' and the next verse says that, seeing no man, He acted with His own arm, Isaiah 59:15-16. The empty search becomes the reason for God's own rescue.

Jeremiah is also placed beside other prophets who stood between God and the people, but whose prayer could no longer save them. Jeremiah 15:1 names Moses and Samuel; Ezekiel 14:14 names Noah, Daniel and Job.

Verses 21 and 22 pass on a stock of wisdom language. The people who have eyes and do not see are the people of Isaiah 6:9-10, and Jesus applies that text to the crowds in Matthew 13:13-15. The boundary of sand answers the question put to Job, 'Who enclosed the sea behind doors?' Job 38:8-11, and recurs in Psalm 104:9.

Paul gathers the whole biblical pattern into one catena in Romans 3:10-18, drawing on Psalm 14 and others, and the word 'truth' of verse 1 returns on Jesus' lips. Verse 14, 'I will make My words a fire in your mouth,' belongs with Jeremiah 20:9 and 23:29, where God's word is a fire and a hammer, not a decoration.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The compiler of this chapter wanted the generation that survived the fall to be able to answer the question the exiles would ask in Babylon, the one verse 19 predicts: 'For what offense has the LORD our God done all these things to us?' The chapter is the prepared answer. It is not a bare list of crimes. It shows that the verdict followed a search, that the city had been offered forgiveness for the price of one honest person, and that God struck with eyes open, hitting a people who 'felt no pain,' verse 3.

The author also wanted hearers to see the shape of Judah's self deception. The people said the right words, 'As surely as the LORD lives,' verse 2, and also said 'He will not do anything,' verse 12. They could swear by God and deny that God acts in the same breath. Verse 31 shows the final stage, in which people do not merely tolerate false prophets but love them. Jeremiah's own hearers were meant to feel the sting of that, and to ask whether they were also paying to be lied to.

The 'not a full end' of verse 18 was meant as the line that holds the exiles up. Judgment would be real and would be explained, but the story would not stop there.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Almost everything in this chapter is description of a particular people at a particular moment: the oaths, the adultery of verses 7 and 8, the fraud of verses 26 to 28. It is not a rule that every nation with injustice in its courts will be invaded within a generation. The promise-and-threat language here was spoken to a covenant people under the terms of Deuteronomy 28, and it should not be lifted onto a modern state as though it were Israel.

What does carry over is the pattern of commands underneath the description. God wants truth in speech, justice for the fatherless and needy, and a heart that fears Him as the giver of rain and harvest. Verse 24 invites believers to the same habit, saying in the heart, 'Let us fear the LORD our God.' Verse 31 is a standing warning for any pulpit or congregation: if the people love flattery, teachers will supply it.

The verse 1 search is not a command to count the righteous. It is the LORD's commission to His prophet, and what it reveals is God's willingness to forgive, not a quota for avoiding His anger.

debates.question: Was forgiveness really on offer in verse 1, or is the search only a way of proving the case?

views.label: A real offer
views.case: The verse is conditional in form: find one, and 'I will forgive.' It echoes Genesis 18, where the same kind of condition was treated as genuine, and Ezekiel 22:30, where God says He looked for one who would stand in the gap in order to avoid destroying. On this view the offer is sincere, and the point is the tragedy that not even one answered it. Verse 7 supports it, since 'Why should I forgive you?' is a question that assumes forgiveness was the desired end.

views.label: A rhetorical demonstration
views.case: Others note that Jeremiah is told in verse 1 to search, and in verses 4 and 5 he tests his own theory, that the poor were ignorant and the great would know better, and fails twice. The search shows the prophet, and the reader, that there is no hidden righteous remnant to appeal to. By chapter 7 he is forbidden to pray for the people at all, Jeremiah 7:16, which suggests the decision was already fixed.

debates.bearing: The two views agree on what matters. God's anger is not hasty, His readiness to forgive is real, and the outcome comes from the people's refusal rather than His reluctance. It is also fair to hold both in tension, as Scripture does when it shows God's open offer and His settled verdict side by side.

debates.question: Who is the 'distant nation' of verse 15?

views.label: Babylon
views.case: The book itself later names Nebuchadnezzar's armies as the instrument, and Habakkuk 1:6 says plainly, 'I am raising up the Chaldeans.' The ancient and established character of the nation fits Mesopotamia, a civilisation older than Judah. Most readers, ancient and modern, take this line.

views.label: A northern horde such as the Scythians
views.case: Some scholars have suggested that the early 'foe from the north' poems, Jeremiah 4 to 6, were first prompted by a wave of nomad raiders in the later seventh century, whom the Greek historian Herodotus describes. The language of an unnamed northern terror in Jeremiah 1:14-15 and 6:22 does not give the nation a name. This view has lost ground, since the Old Testament never mentions Scythians as God's instrument.

debates.bearing: For readers today the question matters less than the pattern. The text deliberately leaves the invader unnamed in the early chapters so that the emphasis falls on who sends him. Whoever marches, the LORD says, 'I am bringing' him, verse 15.

study.originalLanguages:
Verses 1 and 3 name what God is looking for with the word emunah. The BSB translates it 'truth,' and elsewhere it is rendered faithfulness. It comes from the root aman, to be firm or reliable, which is also the root of the word Amen. Emunah is not a set of correct propositions but the quality of a person who can be leaned on. When Jeremiah says in verse 3 that God's eyes look for it, he means that God is hunting for someone who is dependable in the way He is. The same word comes back in Jeremiah 7:28, 'Truth has perished,' where the loss is complete.

The sentence 'refused to repent' in verse 3 is built on two Hebrew verbs, ma'en, to refuse, and shuv, to turn. Both halves of the verse use the verb 'to refuse,' once for discipline and once for turning. The people are not unable, they are unwilling. Shuv is the great verb of Jeremiah's preaching, and he will play on its two meanings in Jeremiah 8:4-5, where turning away and turning back are the same verb.

In verse 12 the BSB's 'He will not do anything' translates a very short Hebrew expression, lo hu, 'not He.' It is a verdict on God Himself, that He is not, in effect, the one who acts. Isaiah records the opposite mockery, 'Let Him hurry and hasten His work so that we may see it,' Isaiah 5:19. Jeremiah's hearers have gone one step further and settled that He will not act at all. The prophets who say so are 'wind,' ruach, a word that can also mean breath or spirit, and the verse ends with the charge that the dabar, the word, is not in them, verse 13.

Verse 15 calls the invader a goy me'olam, an ancient or long standing nation. The word olam is the same word that appears in the 'ancient paths' of Jeremiah 6:16. The nation is ancient, the paths are ancient, and Judah refuses the second so that it will meet the first. In verse 22 the sea's limit is a chuq olam, a perpetual decree, and in verse 24 the harvest weeks are chuqqot, appointed statutes. The language of law is borrowed for the natural order: the sea obeys a decree and the harvest keeps its schedule, while the people who were given statutes do not keep theirs.

Finally, the people of verse 21 are described as 'foolish and senseless,' in Hebrew a people who are sakal and without lev. In Hebrew thought the lev, the heart, is the seat of understanding as much as of feeling, so 'without heart' means without sense. It is the same diagnosis as Jeremiah 4:22, and it explains why verse 24 says they have not said 'in their hearts' to fear the LORD.

typology.type: The empty search for one who acts justly, Jeremiah 5:1
typology.fulfillment: The city could be forgiven for one person of faithfulness, and none could be found. The Bible keeps that question open until a figure appears who is called 'the Righteous One,' Acts 3:14 and 1 John 2:1, the servant who 'will justify many,' Isaiah 53:11. In Christ the correspondence is exact and then overflows: forgiveness is granted to a whole people on the strength of one man's righteousness, Romans 5:19. The type falls short in that the offer of Jeremiah 5:1 is spoken to a single city, while the cross is for those from every nation who believe, and in that Christ was not found in the streets by chance but sent.

typology.type: The sea held back by sand, Jeremiah 5:22
typology.fulfillment: God's authority over the sea is offered as the reason Judah should fear Him. In the Gospels the disciples find the same authority standing in a boat. Jesus 'rebuked the wind and the sea,' and the disciples ask, 'Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?' Mark 4:39-41. The question has an answer in Jeremiah 5:22, Job 38:8-11 and Psalm 104:9: it is the Creator who fixed the boundary. The correspondence is not a coded prediction but a revelation of identity. The type is incomplete because verse 22 leaves the people unmoved, and the disciples' fear only begins their understanding.

typology.type: A nation whose language you do not understand, Jeremiah 5:15
typology.fulfillment: Foreign speech is a sign of judgment here, as it was in Isaiah 28:11, which Paul quotes in 1 Corinthians 14:21: 'By strange tongues and foreign lips I will speak to this people.' At Pentecost the pattern is turned. The Spirit gives the apostles speech that each listener hears 'in his own native language,' Acts 2:6-8. What had been a sign of distance becomes a sign that the gospel reaches those who were far off. The text does not say Acts 2 is the fulfilment of Jeremiah 5:15, so the link is an echo of a theme and not a quotation, but a fair one. The type is limited in that Jeremiah's foreign tongue came with soldiers, and Pentecost's came with a message of forgiveness.

typology.type: 'I will not make a full end of you,' Jeremiah 5:18
typology.fulfillment: The word of verse 18 holds out the survival of a remnant in the middle of destruction. Paul uses the idea in Romans 11:5, 'at the present time there is a remnant chosen by grace.' The remnant is carried by God's choice, not by merit. In Christ the remnant becomes a single person on whom the nation's hope rests, and then a people drawn around Him. The type is incomplete in that the remnant of Jeremiah's day was spared exile's end only after seventy years, while the remnant in Christ is spared eternally.

study.christ:
Jeremiah's search is, at bottom, a search for a person, and the New Testament answers it with a person. Where the prophet found no one who acts justly and seeks truth, the apostles say to Jerusalem, 'You rejected the Holy and Righteous One,' Acts 3:14, and John writes of 'Jesus Christ, the Righteous One,' 1 John 2:1. The Gospel picture is exact: a man walks the streets of Jerusalem who does justice, speaks truth and feeds the poor, and the city, instead of being spared for his sake, takes him out and kills him. The passage's logic is then turned inside out, since forgiveness is given on the strength of that death. 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing,' Luke 23:34, is verse 1's offer, 'then I will forgive the city,' being spent on the very ones who did the killing. Paul says how it works: 'God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God,' 2 Corinthians 5:21.

Truth is the second link. The emunah God looks for in Jeremiah 5:1 shares its root with the word Amen, and Jesus is called 'the Amen, the faithful and true Witness,' Revelation 3:14. John says He is 'full of grace and truth,' John 1:14, and says of Himself, 'I am the way and the truth and the life,' John 14:6. The dependable one that Judah could not produce is given by God.

Isaiah 59 adds a note that deepens it. When the LORD sees that there is no man, His own arm brings salvation, Isaiah 59:16. The failure of the search does not end the story, because God does not wait for a righteous person to appear; He sends one. Jeremiah himself later names Him, 'a righteous Branch,' 'The LORD Our Righteousness,' Jeremiah 23:5-6. Hebrews pictures the intercessor who stands in the gap that Ezekiel 22:30 could not fill: 'He always lives to intercede for them,' Hebrews 7:25.

The 'eyes that do not see' of verse 21 also reach Jesus. He takes the prophets' complaint about blind and deaf Israel and uses it of the crowds who hear His parables, Matthew 13:13-15. The same word of God that Jeremiah was told to make 'a fire in your mouth' is spoken by One who is Himself the Word, John 1:1, and who meets the same hardened hearts.

A caution is in order. Jeremiah 5 is not a hidden prophecy of Jesus' life. It is the Old Testament's most pointed statement of a need. The text makes the need unmistakable and the New Testament shows how God met it, and what it shows is that the answer was never going to be found in Jerusalem's streets, but sent into them.
study.god:
This chapter shows a God whose eyes are always moving. 'Do not Your eyes look for truth?' Jeremiah says in verse 3, and the Chronicler gives the same picture of God: 'The eyes of the LORD move to and fro throughout the earth,' 2 Chronicles 16:9. The search of verse 1 is not the first time God looks. It is the last. He has already struck and disciplined them, verse 3, and they felt nothing. The God who sees is not distant from the injustice of verses 26 to 28; He watches the trap being laid.

He is the Lord of creation, and He uses it as an argument. The sea has an edge that it cannot cross, and each year the autumn and spring rains and the harvest weeks arrive on time. Both are His constant gifts, verse 24, and Jesus will say that the rain falls on the just and unjust alike, Matthew 5:45. Judah's problem is not that God has stopped giving but that they no longer say 'in their hearts' where the gifts come from. Fear in verse 22 is the correct response to creation, an awareness that the one who limits the sea limits kingdoms.

He is just and measured. The devastation is scaled to the sin: those who served foreign gods at home will serve foreigners abroad, verse 19. Even the invasion is held in check: 'do not finish them off,' verse 10, and 'I will not make a full end of you,' verse 18. The same God who says 'Should I not punish them?' twice, verses 9 and 29, says 'Why should I forgive you?' in verse 7 as if wanting to hear a reason.

He is also a God who speaks, and whose word does things. In verse 14 His words become a fire in Jeremiah's mouth and the people become the wood. Jeremiah 23:29 asks, 'Is not My word like fire?' God's speech is not information about what He will do. It is the doing begun.

Finally the chapter holds together two things that are easy to separate: a God of settled covenant promise and a God of living personal response. Because He is faithful to His warnings in Deuteronomy 28:49 He brings the foreign nation, and because He is faithful to His promise He keeps a remnant. For worship, the lesson of verse 24 is plain: thank Him out loud for the rain, and ask Him for the eyes that see.

crossReferences.note: Abraham bargains down from fifty to ten righteous people to save Sodom. Jeremiah's search lowers the number to one and still finds none. The two scenes show how patient God's offers of mercy are and how fully a city can refuse them.

Ezekiel gives the divine view of the same search: God looked for someone to repair the wall and stand in the gap so He would not have to destroy, and found no one. Jeremiah 5:1 and this verse together show that judgment came only after a real search.

Truth stumbles in the public square and honesty cannot enter, just as in Jeremiah's streets. Isaiah then adds what Jeremiah leaves unsaid: seeing no man, the LORD acts with His own arm to save. The empty search becomes the prelude to a rescue.

The LORD looks down to see if any understand and seek God, and finds that all have turned away. Jeremiah's search is this psalm played out in one city's streets, with the poor and the powerful both tested and both found wanting.

Paul strings together psalms and prophets to show that no one is righteous, no one seeks God. Jeremiah 5 is one of the Old Testament witnesses behind the catena, which shows the failure Judah displayed is the human condition, not a local problem.

Moses warned that the LORD would bring a nation from afar whose language Israel would not understand, who would eat their harvest and flocks until they perished. Jeremiah 5:15-17 applies the curse almost line by line, which means the invasion is not a surprise but the covenant being kept.

Habakkuk names the nation Jeremiah leaves unnamed, 'the Chaldeans,' and describes their horses and cavalry swooping like a vulture. Reading the two together shows how the prophets of the same decades saw the same foe, and why Judah could not claim it was not warned.

God asks Job who enclosed the sea behind doors and told it, 'You may come this far, but no farther.' Jeremiah 5:22 uses the same fact against Judah. A people who live beside a sea that obeys should be able to see that the Lord of the sea is not a God to ignore.

Isaiah's commission describes a people ever seeing and never perceiving. Jeremiah's 'eyes but do not see, ears but do not hear' is the same diagnosis, showing that the spiritual blindness of Judah was a pattern across the prophets, not a mood of one generation.

Jesus quotes Isaiah's words to explain why He speaks in parables to a crowd that sees without seeing. The accusation Jeremiah made against Jerusalem is the one Jesus makes against His own hearers, and it shows how long the pattern had run.
Jesus is 'the Amen, the faithful and true Witness.' Amen and the emunah of Jeremiah 5:1 come from the same Hebrew root, so what God searched for in vain in Jerusalem is what Christ is.

God asks whether His word is not like fire and like a hammer that smashes a rock. It shows that the 'fire in your mouth' of 5:14 is not a one off image but the way Jeremiah understood his own message: God's word does what it says.

study.oneStory:
The question this chapter inherits is older than Jeremiah. In Genesis 6 God sees that the thoughts of the human heart are only evil, and He finds one man, Noah, to carry the world through the flood. In Genesis 18 He is willing to spare a whole city for ten. By Jeremiah 5 the search has narrowed to one, and the one does not appear. Every earlier rescue in Scripture depends on God finding someone, and here He finds nobody. The human side of the story has run dry.

What follows from that is not only judgment. The prophets make the dry well into a doorway. Isaiah 59:16 has the LORD looking, finding no one, and acting alone. Ezekiel 22:30 has Him looking for someone to stand in the gap. The Old Testament keeps suspending the question, who will be the righteous one, until Jeremiah 23:5-6 and Isaiah 53:11 name a righteous Branch and a righteous Servant. At the cross the gap is filled, not by finding someone in Jerusalem's streets, but by God entering them.

The chapter also sits in the middle of Israel's own history as a replay of Adam's. Adam was put in a good place with one clear word and a threat of exile, Genesis 3; Judah was put in a good land with the law and the threat of Deuteronomy 28. Both had everything and doubted the Giver. Verse 18's 'I will not make a full end' is the thread that lets the story continue, and it is picked up in Jeremiah 31:31-34 with a new covenant: 'I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts.' That is the cure for the 'stubborn and rebellious hearts' of verse 23.

In the middle of the Bible's plot, then, Jeremiah 5 is a hinge. It gathers the failures of the old order into one city and proves that more commands, more warnings and even better leaders will not change the heart. The answer is the Spirit and the new heart promised in Ezekiel 36:26, and the righteous One who makes forgiveness possible.

The story ends where this chapter's longing is finally met. In the new creation the people in the streets are those who have been made righteous, Revelation 21:27 describes a city where nothing impure enters, and the final question of verse 31, 'what will you do in the end?', is answered for believers by an end that is not exile but the face of God, Revelation 22:4.

quiz.q: What does God ask Jeremiah to search for in Jerusalem's streets?

options.text: A single person who acts justly and seeks the truth, so the city could be forgiven.
options.note: Verse 1 frames this as a genuine search whose failure justifies the coming judgment.

options.text: The wealthiest family in the city.
options.note: The search is about moral and spiritual faithfulness, not wealth.

options.text: The most religious-looking worshippers at the temple.
options.note: The passage explicitly notes that oath-swearing and outward religion did not equal true faithfulness; verse 2 says they swear falsely even while invoking the LORD's name.

options.text: A prophet willing to speak only comforting words.
options.note: The search is for genuine justice and truth, and the chapter later condemns exactly this kind of comfortable false prophecy.

quiz.q: What is the outcome of the search among both the poor and the powerful?

options.text: Both groups alike are found to have broken the yoke and rejected God's ways.
options.note: Verses 4-5 show the search extending from the poor to the powerful, with the same unfaithful result in both cases.

options.text: The poor were found faithful while the powerful were corrupt.
options.note: The text shows both groups equally unfaithful, not one group faithful and the other corrupt.

options.text: The powerful were found faithful while the poor were corrupt.
options.note: This reverses the text; both groups are shown to be equally unfaithful.

options.text: The search was never actually completed.
options.note: The passage explicitly reports the search's outcome for both groups.

quiz.q: How is the coming invading nation described in verses 15-17?

options.text: An ancient, established nation whose language the people do not know or understand.
options.note: Verse 15 emphasizes both its antiquity and its utterly foreign, incomprehensible speech, heightening the sense of dread.

options.text: A small band of local raiders.
options.note: The passage describes a formidable, ancient nation, not a small local group.

options.text: A nation that speaks the same language as Judah.
options.note: The text explicitly says their language is unknown and not understood.

options.text: A peaceful trading partner seeking an alliance.
options.note: The nation is described as devouring harvests and destroying fortified cities, clearly a military threat, not a trading partner.

quiz.q: What does verse 31 reveal about the people's relationship to false prophecy and corrupt priesthood?

options.text: The people actually love having false prophets and self-serving priests.
options.note: The verse states plainly, my people love it so, showing active preference for comfortable lies, not mere passive deception.

options.text: The people were forced against their will to accept false teaching.
options.note: The text explicitly says the people love this arrangement, contradicting the idea of unwilling coercion.

options.text: The people had already rejected all false prophets by this point.
options.note: The verse describes ongoing false prophecy that the people actively love, not rejection of it.

options.text: Only the priests were corrupt while the prophets remained faithful.
options.note: The verse names both prophets and priests together as complicit in this corruption.

quiz.q: How does this chapter's failed search for a righteous person connect to the New Testament?

options.text: Paul's declaration that none is righteous, no, not one, echoes and universalizes this same failed search.
options.note: Romans 3:10-18 draws on this kind of Old Testament pattern to make a global claim about human sinfulness, answered only in Christ.

options.text: It has no meaningful connection to the New Testament.
options.note: Paul's universal indictment in Romans 3 draws directly on this kind of prophetic pattern.

options.text: It shows that some individuals can achieve perfect righteousness on their own.
options.note: The passage and its New Testament echo both emphasize the opposite, universal failure apart from grace.

options.text: It applies only to ancient Jerusalem and has no broader theological significance.
options.note: Its connection to Romans 3 gives it clear broader theological significance about universal sinfulness.

questions: God searched Jerusalem's streets for even one person who lived by truth and justice. If God searched your life the same way this week, what would He find?
Both the poor and the powerful in this chapter were found equally unfaithful. Where do you excuse your own compromises by comparing yourself to a different social group, rich or poor, than your own?
The people preferred comfortable lies from false prophets to hard truth, my people love it so. Where in your own life do you choose comfortable reassurance over hard, needed truth?
God says He will not make a full end even amid severe judgment. Where do you need to trust God's restraint and mercy in consequences you are currently facing?

This chapter's failed search for a righteous person points forward to Christ, the only truly righteous man. How does resting in His righteousness, rather than your own search for goodness, change how you face your own failures this week?

translationNotes.note: Go up through her vineyards uses agricultural imagery for the coming invasion, likening Judah to a vine being stripped rather than uprooted entirely, consistent with the chapter's repeated qualification that judgment, though severe, will not be total.

The image of sand as the sea's unbreakable boundary recalls Job 38:8-11 and Psalm 104:9, both using the same picture of God's fixed limits on chaos as evidence of His power that ought to inspire reverent fear.

Priests rule by their own authority translates language literally closer to at their hands, meaning the priests exercise power on their own terms rather than under God's authority, a picture of religious leadership co-opted for self-interest.
